limits.what: Records every invocation and completion through one counter that all clients share, whose increment is sequentially consistent. A subject whose correctness depends on a memory barrier it lacks can pass under the recorder and fail without it.
limits.why: Goroutines run on more than one core at once. Each increment of the counter orders the recording client's memory operations against every other client's, and that order can supply the barrier that the subject lacks.

limits.what: Compares two functions by their code pointers. Two closures of one function literal compare equal whatever they capture, and so do two method values of one method on different receivers. A function declared at the top level, a method expression and a closure that captures nothing compare exactly. Every assertion that compares values as equal does, and its property form, compares functions the same way.
limits.why: reflect returns a function's code pointer alone, and states that functions with equal code pointers may not behave alike. A closure's identity is the address of its closure object, which only unsafe code reads, and for a function in an unexported field only through the internal layout of reflect.Value. The standard compares fields without unsafe access.

limits.what: Checks the ceiling in an ordinary build. In a build with the race detector, msan or asan, and in a build whose -gcflags turn off optimisation (-N) or inlining (-l), it calls the callable as an ordinary build does and checks no ceiling. It reads those flags from the binary's build information.
limits.why: Those builds allocate differently from the one that ships. Under the race detector sync.Pool drops a quarter of the items it is given, and the compiler's own allocation test counts 8 allocations under -race where the ordinary build makes 1. With inlining off, a constructor returning a pointer allocated once per call where the ordinary build allocated nothing. A ceiling checked there would fail code that meets it. The assertion passes rather than skipping, because a skip would stop every check after it in the caller's test.

limits.what: Checks the ceiling in an ordinary build. In the builds the max-allocs entry names, the contract publishes the count and does not check the ceiling.
limits.why: Those builds allocate differently from the one that ships, as the max-allocs entry states, so a count from such a build does not describe the code.

limits.what: Checks the ceiling in an ordinary build. In the builds the max-allocs entry names, the contract publishes the bytes and does not check the ceiling.
limits.why: Those builds allocate differently from the one that ships, as the max-allocs entry states, so the bytes from such a build do not describe the code.

limits.what: Checks the ceiling for each generated input in an ordinary build. In the builds the max-allocs entry names, it calls the callable for each input and checks no ceiling.
limits.why: The form runs max-allocs on each input, and those builds allocate differently from the one that ships, as the max-allocs entry states.

limits.what: Reads int and uint as 64-bit integers on a 64-bit platform and as 32-bit integers on a 32-bit platform, so one test generates other values on each. ShapeOf writes the width the platform reads. A zone resolves with the platform's time-zone database: the one that ZONEINFO names, the system's, or the copy in the Go installation, which is tzdata 2026c in Go 1.27.1. A time.Time in a zone can then show another wall time than the definition's tzdata 2026e states.
limits.why: The width of a Go int and uint is the platform's word, and a shape states the width of the type it reads. Go reads time zones from the platform, and Go's documentation leaves the choice to embed a database to a program's main package.

limits.what: Decodes a map to a map[any]any, so a map whose key shape decodes to a slice, a map or a record fails to read. A zone resolves with the platform's time-zone database, as the prop.of entry states.
limits.why: A key of a Go map must be comparable, and a slice, a map and the map[string]any of a record are not.

surface.why: A Go assertion is called with the testing.T the test already holds, and outside a test there is no TB at all. A seat that panics on both paths would invent a convention the testing package already owns.
The collector seat is testing.T, which reports through the framework at the end of the test. There is nothing to read back: Errorf has already told the runner.
testing.T flushes itself when the test ends. A flush a caller could invoke would either do nothing or fight the framework.
Go writes a benchmark body inline under testing.B, so a setup closure would take the caller out of both the loop and the chain. It marks the setup in place with Excluding instead.

records.artifact: The event stream that go test -json writes for a run. go test writes the call records under -json and -v alone.
records.location: One attr event per call record. Its Package and Test name the test, its Key is dokimi.assert.<seq>, and its Value is the call record's JSON. A call record whose line does not fit test2json's 4,096-byte line buffer is split over consecutive attr events of the same Key, whose Values join into the call record.
records.status: The pass, fail and skip events of each test.
